implementation_notes: MockK is the Kotlin-native supplier of canned answers: mockk<Warehouse>() builds the double and every { warehouse.hasInventory("Talisker", 50) } returns false programmes the answer, with throws, returnsMany, just Runs and coEvery for suspending functions covering the other shapes of indirect input. Mocks are strict by default, so an unstubbed call fails loudly instead of returning a JVM default - a better fit for stubs than Mockito's null/0/false fallbacks - and relaxed = true opts into permissive defaults when only one call matters. The generated mock replaces a hand-written implementation of the collaborator's interface; where that interface has a single method, a SAM lambda or an object expression is often shorter than the framework.
code_sketch:
val warehouse = mockk<Warehouse>()
every { warehouse.hasInventory("Talisker", 50) } returns false

val order = Order("Talisker", 50)
assertFalse(order.fill(warehouse))   // canned answer, no verify block
pitfalls: Matchers must line up exactly: a stubbed hasInventory("Talisker", 50) does not answer a call with ("Lagavulin", 50), and mixing literals with matchers requires eq() everywhere.
Suspending collaborators need coEvery/coVerify; stubbing a suspend function with every { } can compile in some positions and fail at runtime.
Static/object/constructor mocks (mockkStatic, mockkObject) replace the target globally until unmockkAll or clearMocks runs in teardown.

variants.name: Anonymous object expression implementing the interface
variants.idiom_name: object : Warehouse { override fun ... } with canned returns
variants.implementation_notes: Kotlin's object expressions create an anonymous implementation of the collaborator interface in place - val warehouse = object : Warehouse { override fun hasInventory(sku: String, qty: Int) = false } - which is the classic structure with no library, no reflection and full compiler checking of the overrides. It is the shortest route for one or two canned answers, works in multiplatform and Android unit tests where instrumentation-based mocking is not available, and stays readable because the answer sits next to the assertion. Reach for MockK once several tests need different answers for the same collaborator or the double must also record calls, since rewriting the anonymous object per test is where duplication starts.
pitfalls: An interface with many members forces all of them to be implemented in the object expression; default implementations or a narrower consumer-side interface keep the stub small.
An object expression captured in a val is re-created per test only if it is constructed inside the test (or a fresh fixture); sharing it across tests shares its state.
Object expressions cannot be used where a named factory or JVM-static behaviour is required; those need MockK's static/constructor support instead.
